items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics
items.summary: Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning capabilities to a fast, efficient model built specifically for robotics. To help developers put these capabilities to work, the new Robotics plugin for Google Antigravity transforms the platform into a comprehensive workbench supporting rapid hardware bring-up, MuJoCo simulation, and closed-loop control. Developers can leverage these tools to transition from an unboxed robot arm to a fully functional real-to-sim-to-real application in an afternoon using natural language prompts and day-one support in the google-genai SDKs.

items.title: Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services
items.summary: LiteRT in Google Play services now offers GPU inference powered by ML Drift, delivering about 1.4x faster performance alongside the new CompiledModel API. Switching from bundled binaries reduces app size by approximately 8 MB while enabling seamless, automatic runtime updates across billions of devices. Developers can easily adopt these updates by updating their dependencies and utilizing the new Android Studio LiteRT skill for automated migration.

items.title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
items.summary: A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across web, mobile, and desktop applications. Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. The release introduces bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding to help teams seamlessly integrate generative UI into their product stacks.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: TPU Model Design Considerations and Optimization Guide
items.summary: The newly launched AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide provides hardware-grounded design rules to help developers maximize performance on TPUs for LLMs and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) workloads. Key principles include aligning reduction and output dimensions to 256 for systolic arrays, adopting LatentMoE to compress routed token traffic, and mapping parallel axes directly onto physical links.

items.title: Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation
items.summary: This post walks through the Agents CLI evaluation loop for systematically improving agent performance through continuous testing and grading. It demonstrates how to catch prompt regressions, evaluate model backend swaps using side-by-side trace comparisons, and automate evaluation passes. Developers will also learn how to integrate nightly scheduled runs with threshold-based alerting to track quality over time.

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection (AAD) provides asynchronous, low-latency monitoring for AI agents by analyzing OpenTelemetry traces and logs to flag goal hijacks and tool misuse. Tested across five public security benchmarks, AAD successfully caught 87% of harmful instructions carried out by agents without adding runtime latency. Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

items.title: Securing Your Agents: A Hands-On Guide to Agent Anomaly Detection
items.summary: This guide walks developers through setting up Agent Anomaly Detection on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform to monitor AI agent telemetry and catch behavioral risks. It demonstrates how to deploy a sample customer support agent, trigger out-of-scope security findings, and configure proactive alerts using Cloud Monitoring and Security Command Center.

items.title: From prompt to app: Build with Google Maps in AI Studio
items.summary: Developers can now build applications powered by Google Maps Platform directly within Google AI Studio by prompting Gemini with real-world geospatial concepts. The integration eliminates traditional configuration hurdles by providing one-click demo keys that generate instantly without requiring Cloud Console redirects or credit cards. This setup grants developers immediate access to core APIs—including Maps, Places, and Routes—supported by daily sandbox quotas for seamless prototyping.

items.title: Estados de email accesibles en React
items.summary: Un formulario de registro puede parecer terminado cuando el usuario pulsa “Crear cuenta”. En realidad, ahí empieza una parte delicada: enviar el email, esperar la respuesta, mostrar el resultado y permitir que la persona continúe sin adivinar qué ocurrió. En proyectos React he encontrado que este flujo se trata aveces como un detalle visual. Un spinner aparece, el botón se desactiva y, si todo va bien, llega un mensaje verde. Ese enfoque falla cuando el correo tarda, cuando el usuario navega con teclado o cuando un lector de pantalla no recibe el cambio. La interfaz necesita un modelo de estados explícito, no solo una animación. Un estado de email tiene al menos cinco momentos útiles: Inicial: todavía no se ha enviado nada. Enviando: la petición está en curso y no debe duplicarse. Esperando: el servidor aceptó la solicitud, pero el mensaje aún no ha sido confirmado. Verificado: el enlace fue aceptado y el flujo puede continuar. Error: la persona necesita una explicación y una acción posible. Separar “enviando” de “esperando” mejora la experiencia. items.title: Three Booleans Is Not a State Machine: Modelling UI Logic That Can't Be in Two States at Once
items.summary: I review a lot of component code. The most common bug pattern I see is not a typo. It is this: const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false); const [isError, setIsError] = useState(false); const [isSuccess, setIsSuccess] = useState(false); Three booleans, eight combinations, three of which are legal. The other five are bugs waiting for a slow network. Everyone knows not to set isLoading and isSuccess at the same time. Nobody sets them deliberately. They happen because the flags are set in different places, on different async paths, sometimes in an await that resolves after the component re-rendered. Add a quantity and a retryCount and the handshake gets worse. Add a "pending but optimistic" case and you have invented a fourth flag, and now four booleans give you sixteen states where five are legal. This is the classic argument for a discriminator: type Status = | { kind: "idle" } | { kind: "validating" } | { kind: "submitting"; optimistic: boolean } | { kind: "error"; message: string; retryable: boolean } | { kind: "success"; orderId: string }; One variable, five states, no illegal combinations by construction. items.title: Object Storage and Signed URLs for Tenant-Isolated SaaS Exports Explained
items.summary: Short answer: For most SaaS report exports, put the generated file in object storage and return a short-lived signed download URL. That keeps large transfers away from the Node.js app server and makes tenant boundaries explicit in the object key. Keeping PDFs on instance disk can work for a prototype, but it couples delivery to one machine and makes scaling and cleanup somebody's Friday problem. The decision is less about finding the lowest per-gigabyte number and more about choosing a failure boundary you can operate. I've learned to write the rule down: one export gets one immutable key, one authorization check, and one presigned GET. Measure download latency, storage growth, and failed authorization attempts before copying the pattern across every report type. Keep it boring. Imagine a media SaaS with tenants acme and northstar. The export worker writes exports/{tenantId}/{reportId}.pdf; the API only presigns a key after checking that the requesting user belongs to that tenant. The browser receives the URL, while the application server never streams the PDF bytes. That layout fixes two practical problems at once. items.title: How to export a ChatGPT conversation to Markdown, DOCX or print — the manual way first
items.summary: ChatGPT lets you share a conversation as a link, and it lets you export all of your data at once. What it does not have is a simple "save this one conversation as a file" button. If you need a single conversation as Markdown, DOCX or a printable page, here are the options that work today — manual first, then what I am building to automate it. Select the text of the conversation, copy it, and paste it into a Markdown editor or a word processor. Works for short conversations. Loses most formatting: code blocks, headings and links usually come across as plain text, and you have to rebuild them by hand. For a long conversation, scrolling and selecting the whole thread is slow and error-prone. Good enough if you do this once in a while. Open the conversation, press Ctrl+P (Cmd+P on macOS), and choose "Save as PDF". Keeps the layout roughly as it appears on screen. You get a PDF, not Markdown or DOCX, so the text is not easy to edit or re-use afterwards. Long conversations print fine, but page breaks can split code blocks. items.title: pnpm Workspaces vs Turborepo vs Nx: Do You Need a Monorepo Build Tool?
items.summary: Short answer: if your monorepo has fewer than roughly a handful of packages and CI finishes in a few minutes, pnpm workspaces alone are enough. Add Turborepo when you want cached, dependency-ordered task running with almost no configuration. Reach for Nx when you need project-graph tooling, code generators, or enforced module boundaries, and you accept a larger surface area to learn. This post is written for the moment you search "do I need Turborepo" after your CI time started creeping up. Tool details are as of November 2026; the decision logic should survive the next releases. A surprising amount. Declare the packages and you get linked local dependencies, a single lockfile, and recursive or filtered script execution. # pnpm-workspace.yaml packages: - "apps/*" - "packages/*" # run "build" in every package, dependencies first (topological order) pnpm -r build # only the web app and everything it depends on pnpm --filter web... build # only packages changed since main, plus their dependents pnpm --filter "...[origin/main]" test That last command is the one people miss. items.title: GSAP vs a Motion Runtime: Why 'Which Is Better' Is the Wrong Question
items.summary: Every comparison post about GSAP starts the same way: a table with checkmarks, where the author's tool has all of them. Let me try a more useful framing. GSAP is a library you call. Exode is an environment that writes code which calls things. Those are different rungs of the stack. You can use both. You cannot meaningfully replace one with the other, and most teams that try end up with a worse version of what they had. I have shipped GSAP in production for years. It is fast, it is stable, and the timeline API is still the best mental model for sequencing in JavaScript: const tl = gsap.timeline({ defaults: { ease: "power3.out" } }); tl.from(".card", { y: 24, opacity: 0, stagger: 0.06 }) .to(".price", { scale: 1.04, duration: 0.18, yoyo: true, repeat: 1 }, " name === "addToCart" && handleAdd()} /> Tuned by dragging sliders. Reviewed as a JSON diff plus a rendered snapshot in CI. The difference is not capability. It is who can do the tuning and where the source of truth lives. Maturity. GSAP has been in production for over a decade. Its edge cases are known, its docs are excellent, and it runs in every browser you care about. Exode is younger; you will hit rough edges. No format. items.title: Why We Ditched Pendo for Open-Source Product Tours in Our Codebase
items.summary: The Pendo Problem You know the feeling. Your product tour works fine until your designer wants to tweak the copy. You log into Pendo's dashboard, make the change, wait for it to deploy, and hope nothing breaks in production. Then someone asks, "When did we change that tour?" and you're stuck digging through dashboards instead of git history. And the pricing? Pendo charges per active user. Your SaaS grows, your bill grows faster. That's intentional design on their part. But it shouldn't be. We hit the ceiling when our team kept asking: Why does this live outside our codebase? Why can't we test it? Why do we need a separate tool? Product tours are features. They're not some untouchable third-party service. They deserve the same treatment as your other features: version control, code review, CI/CD integration, and testing. When tours live in your codebase, something magical happens: Version control becomes your audit trail. Need to know why a tour step was reworded? Check the commit. Who approved it? Look at the PR. items.summary: Falha na Optimizely levou malware a sites de 178 organizações Uma vulnerabilidade na ferramenta Experimentation da Optimizely foi explorada para inserir JavaScript malicioso em projetos de clientes. Os códigos chegaram aos visitantes de sites de organizações como BBC, IKEA, Zoom, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, HSBC, Equifax, Ledger e Air France-KLM. O pesquisador Scott Helme, fundador da plataforma Report URI, encontrou 188 arquivos infectados entre 1.611 arquivos da Optimizely que analisou. A estimativa é de 178 organizações afetadas. O incidente ocorreu em 16 de novembro de 2026, e o total pode ser maior. Clientes da Optimizely usam pequenos arquivos JavaScript fornecidos pela plataforma para testar versões de páginas e personalizar sites. Os invasores alteraram projetos de clientes, e os servidores da empresa continuaram entregando os arquivos adulterados aos navegadores como se fossem componentes legítimos. Helme identificou três versões do código. Algumas redirecionavam os navegadores a um domínio controlado pelos criminosos; outras ocultavam o endereço por codificação ou carregavam uma cópia do malware diretamente na página. items.title: Why I Chose Node.js Queue Caps: 3 Latency Guards for Insurance Claims Retrieval
items.summary: Short answer: bound queue wait, concurrent retrieval work, and total request time before tuning ranking quality for insurance claims intake. A fast retriever with an unbounded waiting room still misses its latency budget under load, while a bounded system can make an explicit choice between admitting more work and preserving useful evidence for requests already in flight. I started with one broad vector search because the diagram was tidy. The more important design correction wasn't another retrieval stage; it was recognizing that every query shared the same finite execution capacity. Policy-number lookups, long loss narratives, and reranking requests could all compete for it. Once that happens, a per-request stopwatch measures only part of the problem. The three guards I now design around are admission, concurrency, and deadline. They don't guarantee retrieval quality, and they aren't benchmark results. They make the quality-versus-latency decision visible enough to test with the claims data and traffic shape that actually matter. Start at the user-visible boundary and work backward. items.title: Rive vs Exode: Two Very Different Answers to the Same Word, 'State Machine'
items.summary: "State machine" has become one of those words that means whatever the vendor needs it to mean. Rive and Exode both use it. They are not describing the same thing, and understanding the difference will save you a migration. Rive's state machine lives inside an animation. You have a character or a vector artwork, and you define states for the artwork: idle → hover when the pointer enters idle → pressed on click any → success when a boolean input flips Inputs are typed, transitions have conditions and blend durations, and the runtime advances the machine every frame. It is excellent. It is also scoped to the artboard: the machine cannot position your page, choose a layout, or read from your application store unless you pass values in as inputs. That is not a limitation of Rive's engineering. It is the correct scope for its job: making a .riv artwork react. Exode's state machine sits above the scene, not inside one piece of art. It owns application-level state — idle, validating, submitting, error, success — and it can: drive multiple objects at once, not just one artwork read and write typed variables (boolean, number, string, colour) fire listeners that trigger animations, navigation

items.title: Deletion Deadlines Explained: 429 Queue Backoff for Node.js AI Image Object Storage
items.summary: Short answer: keep image generation and object storage as separate queue steps, persist the generated bytes, and retry each step with exponential backoff; use an idempotent object key so a 429 rate limit or upload timeout cannot create a second artifact. That rule also works for a marketplace that stores signed documents and must delete them on a deadline. An AI image is just a different payload. The durable sink is useful only when the handoff is explicit: a worker records the generation result, then another worker owns the upload and retention metadata. Treat the generated bytes as an input to a new job, not as a reason to call the image model again. The first worker writes a short-lived local or database-backed blob reference with the job id. The upload worker derives marketplace/{jobId}.png (or a document key with the same deterministic pattern), checks whether that key already exists, and then performs the write. A retry sees the same key and the same payload. Here is a minimal TypeScript worker using the two verified storage routes. items.title: IAsyncEnumerable Streaming
items.summary: Streaming" width="800" height="1000"> During a recent performance audit of our reporting APIs, I tracked down erratic Gen2 GC pauses to a seemingly innocent endpoint. The code called .ToListAsync() on a massive table containing over 50,000 historical transaction records before returning an Ok(list) response. This approach forces ASP.NET Core to allocate the entire result set in memory, doubling or tripling allocations during JSON serialization and locking up thread pool resources. [HttpGet("reports")] public async Task GetReports() { var list = await db.Orders.ToListAsync(); return Ok(list); // buffers all rows in RAM } By leveraging IAsyncEnumerable straight from Entity Framework Core, we bypass the intermediate list allocation entirely. The ASP.NET Core framework understands this interface and immediately streams the records down the HTTP response pipe as data flows from the underlying SQL Server data reader. [HttpGet("reports")] public IAsyncEnumerable GetReports() { return db.Orders.AsAsyncEnumerable(); } Heap Allocations: Bypasses temporary List backing arrays, keeping memory usage flat regardless of row count. items.title: The tests were green, a person found the hole: a vulnerability in our OpenID server, start to finish
items.summary: How many green tests does it take to believe a protection works? We have about two thousand, and they pass on three databases. A person still found the hole: an outside researcher who worked through our server and saw a connection where we had seen none. This is the story of GHSA-vmj2-8phj-mfxf in redb.Identity, our OAuth 2.1 / OpenID Connect server for .NET. In order and with dates: what was broken, why we did not see it ourselves, how we fixed it and how we disclosed it. On 4 November a private report on version 4.6.1 came in. Its author, Rathnadeepan (HotWater, HotWater-015 on GitHub), did not open a public issue or write a blog post about it. He wrote to us directly and left us time to fix it. We checked the report against the source the same day. It was all true. A plain access token is accepted from anyone who presents it. If it is stolen from a log, a proxy or an intermediate node, it can be used. DPoP (RFC 9449) changes that by binding the token to the client's key. items.title: Building a Resume Editor That Exports Real Text: A4 Layout, Vector PDFs and DOCX
items.summary: On paper, building a resume editor sounds like a weekend project. You throw together a two-column layout: form inputs on the left, a live preview on the right, and a shiny "Download PDF" button up top. Simple, right? Except it almost never is. The moment a user actually relies on your tool to apply for a job, expectations skyrocket. They expect the exported file to mirror the on-screen preview pixel for pixel. They expect it to fit neatly onto standard A4 paper without awkward blank gaps. They want the typography intact. And most importantly: they expect the output to be a living, breathing document—one with selectable, copyable text that applicant tracking systems (ATS) can actually parse, and maybe even a Word (.docx) file they can tweak later. While building Pagewise, I quickly realized a fundamental truth that reshaped how I approached the entire architecture: A document that looks great in a web browser isn’t guaranteed to survive printing, PDF parsing, or external word processors. items.title: Node.js Express Storage: Store Generated Images in Per-User Folders with Lifecycle Deletes
items.summary: A marketplace that retains signed documents has two different clocks: the access-control clock (who may read an object now) and the deletion clock (when it must disappear). Treating a user folder as both creates a quiet compliance failure. Short answer: keep authorization in Node.js and Express, keep each object private under a tenant-scoped key, record delete_at in a database, and use lifecycle automation as a backstop that you can observe. items.title: Accepted Bid Telemetry — Broadcast Sequence Boundaries for Client Trust
items.summary: Accept bids through the application server, commit their sequence numbers, and keep typing indicators and read receipts outside that authority boundary. Short answer: publish accepted state after the transaction commits; use sequence gaps to trigger recovery, and give clients only the authority required for their conversation. Arrival order cannot decide the winning bid. For a developer tool that embeds an auction discussion panel, the awkward boundary is between a temporary typing signal, a durable receipt, and an accepted high bid. They may share a screen. They should not share an unrestricted credential or an undifferentiated retention policy. This decision record evaluates that boundary through telemetry volume, client trust, and the work required to carry a committed event into delivery. The server decides bid order. It assigns an incrementing sequence number to accepted state, commits that state, and then publishes it. A client seeing sequence 108 after 106 has evidence of a gap; it does not have evidence that 107 never existed. Recovery must consult authoritative application state. Frame one shows your application's sidebar. Frame twelve captures a modal mid-transition. The encoder did exactly what you asked—it rendered the HTML you gave it, including the preview interface you forgot was part of the DOM tree. This is the failure mode I am addressing while evaluating heygen-com/hyperframes. Its premise, "Write HTML. Render video," makes HTML the production artifact. A preview dialog, responsive sidebar, or entrance animation must never quietly become part of that artifact. For a React application using Tailwind CSS v4 and Radix primitives, my recommendation is straightforward: isolate the render document, and animate only the surrounding interface. The architecture has three responsibilities. The application produces a self-contained HTML document. The preview interface displays that document without modifying it. items.title: School Phone Bans Are Gradually Improving Test Scores
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: School cellphone bans are beginning to modestly improve students' academic performance, according to the first large national analysis that compared students' test scores before and after the bans. Schools with strict bans -- requiring students to lock their phones in pouches all school day -- saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year, the study found. It was published Tuesday by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard. U.S. students' test scores began falling over a decade ago. The drop coincided with the rise of smartphones, raising questions about their role in the decline. The evidence so far on the academic effects of phone bans has been mixed. But the new study indicates they are starting to have an influence. The study looked at 3.3 million students between 2021 and 2026. They were in third through 10th grade, attending 4,600 U.S. schools. Using scores on MAP tests, which track achievement from fall to spring, it compared the performance of students at schools that put in strict phone bans with those at similar schools that did not have such bans.

items.title: React Server Components vs. Client Components: Choosing the Right Boundary
items.summary: When building with Next.js App Router, it's tempting to add "use client" to a page as soon as one component needs state or event handlers. But that decision can affect the client-side module graph and the JavaScript the browser needs to load. A more deliberate approach is to separate server-side responsibilities from browser-dependent interactions. For example, a product page might use: A Server Component for fetching and displaying product information. A Client Component for selecting product variations. A Client Component for cart interactions. Server Components for related product content. The exact boundaries depend on the application's needs. Server Components aren't automatically better for every situation, and Client Components aren't inherently bad. The important thing is to understand what each component needs to do. items.title: Detect Known VPN Traffic in Express and FastAPI Middleware
items.summary: A spike hits /account. Half the requests look scripted. Someone on the team suggests a one-line fix: block every VPN. That rule is tempting, and it is a good way to lock out people on a company VPN or a privacy relay, while anyone determined just switches networks. A better pattern is middleware that looks up the client IP, attaches a few flags to the request, and steps up verification on sensitive paths. Log it, tighten a rate limit, or send a challenge. Don’t hard-block by default, and don’t treat a flag as a verdict that someone is hiding something. This post is that middleware in Express and in FastAPI. A longer walkthrough, including a few more edge cases, is in the guide to detecting VPN traffic in Node.js and Python. One GET /v0/ip/{ip} call, with Authorization: Bearer, returns location, network and traits. This is not proxy detection. On a paid key, the traits that matter for live traffic are: is_vpn — the IP belongs to a known VPN network, including major commercial VPN providers. items.title: AI Image Generation: Saving PNG Buffers to Compatible Object Storage
items.summary: Short answer: decode the generated image exactly once into a Node.js Buffer, verify that it is a PNG, then save that binary buffer with Content-Type: image/png to compatible object storage; reject malformed base64 before an upload is attempted. An image worker should treat its decoded PNG as a separate artifact before it writes to compatible object storage. The operational constraint is simple: a successful object write proves that bytes arrived, not that the bytes were a valid generated PNG. Make decoding and PNG validation a local, deterministic step; upload the resulting Node.js Buffer only after it passes. That choice prevents malformed base64 errors from being misdiagnosed as storage failures, and it keeps retry budgets attached to the network operation that can actually benefit from a retry. Start by naming the representation at the API boundary. An image generator can return ordinary base64 text, a data URL such as data:image/png;base64,..., or a remote URL. Those are three different contracts. Only the decoded bytes are suitable as the body of an object write. The problem was real before the architecture became complicated The first version was an ASP.NET Core application with a browser interface and JSON-based persistence. Alongside the account and payment workflows, I developed reminders and a routine for operating the application on my own Linux infrastructure. Later, I wanted to support individual logins and multiple families, each with its own accounts, payments, settings and permissions. That raised a more difficult question: How could I add a multi-family architecture without putting an application I already relied on at unnecessary risk? Keep a working baseline working I chose to evolve the system incrementally. The documented baseline retained the original JSON store while PostgreSQL, EF Core and individual identity support were developed separately. items.title: BugMeNot Calls It Quits
items.summary: BugMeNot, the password-sharing service launched in 2003 to help users bypass website registration requirements, has shut down without explanation after more than two decades. All that's left on the website is a farewell message that reads: "Thanks to everyone who envisioned a better internet." heise online reports: Founded by Guy King, the service had been online since 2003: BugMeNot was a collection of login credentials for various online services. Volunteers submitted credentials they had created for different websites. The idea was simple: Nobody wants to create a full account and provide all their sensitive information just to use a service occasionally. Two decades ago, this privacy concern was more firmly embedded in the public consciousness, but it has since faded considerably. Back then, usernames and passwords were usually the only access controls, so people could easily submit those credentials. Multifactor authentication was still exotic, and passkeys were a distant prospect. The once-popular service lost its shine after just a few years. items.title: Stop Client User Spoofing in React Telegram Mini Apps with Backend HMAC Check
items.summary: Building a Telegram Mini App inside React feels straightforward: Telegram provides a native JavaScript script, developers load it, pull the user object from window.Telegram.WebApp.initDataUnsafe.user, and render a custom storefront or checkout interface. However, relying on initDataUnsafe for backend transactions opens a severe security vulnerability. The initDataUnsafe object is unverified front-end state. Anyone opening your Mini App in Telegram Desktop, a browser, or a custom webview can open Developer Tools or intercept network requests to override window.Telegram.WebApp.initDataUnsafe.user.id with any arbitrary user ID. If your React app sends that unverified user.id to your backend checkout endpoint, an attacker can place orders, view private data, or deplete account balances under another user's identity. To build a secure Mini App, you must transmit the raw, untouched initData query string to your server, verify its HMAC-SHA256 signature using your Telegram Bot Token, check the payload timestamp to block replay attacks, and only then enable native UI controls like the MainButton. Open Folio Everyday PDF jobs are small: join two files, shrink one to fit an upload limit, turn a scan into searchable text, sign a form. I wanted one place that does all of them without an account or a payment step, and an editor that changes the words already on the page instead of only drawing new ones on top. One tool is one Python function. Every tool is run(inputs, options, out_dir) that returns the output files, registered with its title, category, accepted file types and an option schema. The React front end draws each tool's options from that schema, so adding a tool means one function and one registry entry, with no new page to build. items.title: Stop the agent from wrapping every handler in useMemo “for performance”
items.summary: The PR “cleans up” a form by wrapping every event handler in useCallback and every derived boolean in useMemo. The commit message says “performance.” There is no profile, no skipped render that mattered, and two stale-closure bugs in the validation path. I’ve started treating agent-added useMemo / useCallback without a stated reason as noise, not as an optimization. React is not cheaper just because the call site looks official. The wrappers are extra dependencies to get wrong. The model has been trained on a lot of “always memoize callbacks passed to children” advice. Some of that advice was aimed at class components, or at a child wrapped in memo that actually sits in a hot list. A one-off in a settings page is not that situation. useMemo also lies about cost. Memoizing a boolean const isEmpty = items.length === 0 is slower to think about than the comparison. Memoizing a big filtered list can be real — if the input is large and the parent renders often. That sentence should be in the PR, not implied by the hook. Stale closures show up when the dependency array omits a function or a piece of form state. The memo was added to help, and now a submit handler sees yesterday’s values.

items.title: Muting the mic for every app on macOS with Core Audio
items.summary: Zoom, Teams and Meet each have their own mute, and they don't know about each other. I wanted one hotkey that mutes the mic for everything, so I made a small menu bar app for it. It sets kAudioDevicePropertyMute on the input devices through Core Audio, so every app just gets silence. By default it mutes all inputs, not only the default one, because Zoom and Meet often disagree about which mic is "the" mic. It also listens for changes and puts the mute back if some app flips it. ⌘⇧M toggles it, and there's push to talk too. Later I added optional local recording of the mic plus system audio into one small file, which is handy for dropping a call into ChatGPT or Claude for a summary. It's free and MIT, macOS 14+: github.com/oochernyshev/lockmic. I'm the developer, happy to answer Core Audio questions.

items.summary: I have been scraping catalogs, prices, product cards and listings for years. All that time a small homegrown HTML parser did the work: millions of pages, no complaints. It never went public because its tests covered only my own sites and there were no docs. Last week I cleaned it up and released it as z3l.FastHtmlParser. The first version answered "how do I find a tag fast". Since then it has gone through five releases in one week, driven by feedback: XPath 1.0, CSS selectors, a review against hostile markup, and parsing straight from a char[] buffer. This post covers the idea, the numbers and the trade-offs. dotnet add package z3l.FastHtmlParser In a high-volume scraping service the parser is the hottest loop, and your server bill grows with it. HtmlAgilityPack and AngleSharp are excellent libraries, but they are built to be browsers. They create an object for every node, synthesize the implicit , and , and keep a mutable tree so you can edit it and walk it with selectors. A scraper does far less: find an element, read its text or an attribute, move on. So the idea is simple: don't build what you won't use. items.title: How to check a license key in your Mac app offline
items.summary: Short answer: Sign each license on your server with Ed25519, then verify it in the app with CryptoKit and the matching public key. Honest customers stay unlocked offline, because the check does not need a network call. Verify the signature and the expiry at launch and again where the paid feature runs, not in a single isLicensed() flag. A shared serial list, or a secret compiled into the app, can be copied out of the binary. Anyone who has that secret can invent keys your app will accept, or share one serial widely. AI tools make that read faster than it used to be. A signed license works the other way around. Your server holds a private key and signs a small payload: the customer's email, the product name, and an expiry. The app ships the public key and uses it to verify the signature. The public key cannot issue a new license. Sign the raw payload bytes. Then ship the payload and the signature as standard Base64, joined by a period: base64(payload) + "." + base64(signature) The payload is JSON, for example: {"email":"customer@example.com","product":"MyApp","expiry":"2027-11-17T00:00:00Z"} Leave the payload machine-agnostic unless you have a clear reason to bind a device, so the s

items.title: System.Threading.Channels in .NET 10, Measured: The Write Said True and the Item Was Gone
items.summary: System.Threading.Channels in .NET 10, Measured: The Write Said True and the Item Was Gone When a producer is faster than its consumer, something has to give. The queue between them can grow without limit, the producer can be made to wait, or items can be thrown away. System.Threading.Channels makes you pick one of those, which is exactly what it should do. What surprised me is how two of the choices report it: a bounded channel in a drop mode answers true to the write of an item it has just thrown away. I measured an unbounded channel and all four modes of a bounded one under the same load on .NET 10, then broke a three-stage pipeline in the middle to see who notices. Short answer: nobody, unless every stage is wired to tell the others. Every example below is a .NET 10 file-based app: save the block as a .cs file and run it with dotnet run -c Release .cs, with no project file. The numbers come from .NET 10.0.15 on an 8-core laptop. items.title: Staying hands-on while leading delivery
items.summary: Hands-on leadership does not mean taking every difficult ticket. It means staying close enough to the code and production path to make sound decisions, while giving the team clear ownership of the work. The examples come from Zotic, Amlaak, Happy Ticket, Project Pavilion and Alreef. Architecture, planning, review, and deployment are often treated as separate responsibilities. In practice, each one corrects the others. A deployment exposes operational constraints. Those constraints change an architecture decision. The decision changes how work should be sliced. Code review shows whether the slice was clear enough. A lead who never touches that loop can make decisions based on diagrams that no longer match the system. A lead who keeps all hard implementation work has the opposite problem: the team waits for one person and never gains ownership. A short decision note is usually enough. State the problem, the constraints, the chosen approach, the alternatives that were considered, and what would cause the choice to be revisited. The purpose is not documentation volume. items.title: How InkHammy checks grammar in every Mac app with the Accessibility API
items.summary: I'm Zak, and I build InkHammy, a grammar checker that runs as a Mac menu bar app and as an iPhone keyboard. Disclosure up front: InkHammy is my product. This post isn't a review; it's a write-up of how the Mac app reads and fixes text inside other apps through the macOS Accessibility API, and the design choices that came out of it. A browser extension only sees web pages. A lot of writing on a Mac happens somewhere else: Slack, Mail, Notes, Messages, the ChatGPT app, and text fields inside desktop apps built on web views. To check text in all of them, an app has to follow whichever field has focus, read its text, know where each word sits on screen, and write corrections back without breaking the host app. macOS exposes this through the Accessibility API (AX). The user grants Accessibility permission once in System Settings, and the app can then observe and act on UI elements in other processes. AX is powerful, but every host app implements it a little differently, and a call into a busy app can block. Most of InkHammy's Mac architecture exists to deal with those two facts. items.title: Why I took Whisper out of my iPhone transcription app before it shipped
items.summary: I work on Koedori at W Lab. It is an iPhone app that records a lecture, a meeting or an interview and turns it into text on the phone itself, with no account, and the audio is never uploaded. The early builds ran Whisper through WhisperKit. The version on the App Store has no Whisper in it at all: it uses Apple's SpeechAnalyzer framework and its SpeechTranscriber module. This post is about why, and what building on SpeechTranscriber is like. Koedori makes three promises: transcription is free and needs no account, audio never leaves the phone, and re-transcribing costs nothing, as often as you like. The second one is architecture, not a setting. There is no code path that uploads audio, and the app has no server of its own. So recognition has to run on the device, and it has to be cheap enough to run again on a whim. Whisper on the phone met that on paper. The trouble was everything around the model. WhisperKit compiles a model for the Neural Engine the first time it loads it. On the iPhone 14 I measured, the first load of large-v3 turbo after an install took 197 to 205 seconds, every time. A reload within the same install took 4 seconds, and a 10-second clip then transcribed in 0.

From the report: [California Attorney General Rob Bonta] cited the "infamous" incident in July, where two OpenAI models broke out of a testing environment, gained unauthorized access to the open internet, and breached the internal systems of open-source developer platform Hugging Face. OpenAI said the models were trying to find information that they could use to cheat on an evaluation, and succeeded. The break-in at Hugging Face, which Nvidia acquired for roughly $13 billion in September, rattled industry researchers and prompted government officials to call for more stringent oversight of the AI industry. On Monday, Bonta said that OpenAI later disclosed to his investigators that it was aware of 80 incidents "involving loss of control and access to third-party networks and websites." items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Just 400 hyperscale data centers connected in the US used as much electricity as the state of Michigan in a single year, new Harvard research has found. The study, published Monday in Nature Sustainability, also finds that the majority of that electricity was generated using fossil fuels, and data center emissions are three times higher than they were before the AI boom. Federal and state governments do not track data center use separate from the rest of the power sector, despite mounting projections that data centers are putting serious strain on the American power grid. Individual data centers' power use is often considered proprietary business information, and data center operators and utilities do not have to disclose specific numbers to the public. The Harvard study specifically focuses on hyperscale data centers -- the largest types of facilities, which have become flashpoints in community opposition across the country. While often used for AI inference or training, not all of the hyperscalers surveyed in this study are being used for AI. "Comcast should be required to restore to AT&T any and all profits earned as a result of its false and misleading advertising or provide AT&T with any other restitutionary relief the Court deems appropriate," the lawsuit said. Ars Technica reports: While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. items.title: FBI Says Artex AI Open-Source Hacking Tool Used to Breach Networks In 'Under Three Hours'
items.summary: The FBI is warning (PDF) that hackers are using the AI-powered penetration-testing tool Artex to compromise networks in "under three hours" in some cases. The tool has been linked to attacks against South Korean financial institutions, at least 2,250 ConnectWise customers and Barracuda. TechCrunch reports: Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network's defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be "noisy," meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company's defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that makes it far more harder for human defenders to keep up. In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise "in under three hours." Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim's network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. items.title: I built a Mac menu bar app that rewrites text in any app
items.summary: I kept doing the same thing ten times a day: copy a Slack message into a chat window, ask for "more professional" or "shorter", copy the answer, paste it back. So I built Quill, a small macOS menu bar app that does the round trip for me. Select text in any app, press ⌃⌥Space, pick a prompt, and the rewrite replaces your selection. Undo still works, because Quill pastes through the app's own paste. Prompts: Fix Grammar, Professional, Shorter and Friendly to start. You can add, edit, reorder and delete them, or type a one-off instruction. Direct shortcuts: any prompt can have its own global shortcut, which rewrites the selection without opening the popup. No selection: Quill rewrites the whole text field. Model: it uses your own Groq API key with openai/gpt-oss-20b. It's written in SwiftUI and AppKit, with no third-party dependencies, and needs macOS 14 or later. The hard part isn't the AI call. It's reading and writing text in someone else's app, safely. Quill registers system-wide hotkeys with Carbon, which still works, and needs no extra permission for this. One shortcut opens the popup. Each prompt can have its own. items.title: White-Label iOS Architecture: One Codebase, Many Brands
items.summary: Most articles about white-label mobile apps stop at “use build configurations for your colors.” That advice survives about three brands. The problems that decide whether a white-label program is maintainable show up somewhere around the eighth: release trains that no longer fit in a sprint, a test matrix nobody can run, and feature code slowly filling with the name of one particular brand. This is a structural guide to shipping one Swift codebase as many branded apps: what belongs in configuration, what belongs in code, how the Xcode project is wired, and which decisions are expensive to reverse once you have store listings in production. It assumes native iOS. items.title: Your iOS App Says “Offline”—But Is It? Debugging API Failures With a VPN Enabled
items.summary: A user connects their iPhone to a VPN, opens your app and sees: No internet connection. Please try again. They switch to another app, which works. Your app may have encountered a real failure. But “no internet” might be the wrong diagnosis. A hostname lookup can fail. A secure connection can fail. An API can return an authentication error. The response can arrive successfully and then fail JSON decoding. A failed API operation does not automatically mean the device is offline—or that the VPN caused the failure. The first useful fix is to preserve those distinctions in your networking code. Think of an API operation as several stages: Establish a usable network connection. Resolve the destination hostname when needed. Establish the secure connection. Exchange the HTTP request and response. Interpret the response body. This is a debugging model, not a claim that every request creates a new connection or performs a fresh DNS lookup. Connections and lookup results can be reused. The point is that failures at different stages need different handling. items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
items.summary: A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone. That means that (a+b)+c is not always equal to a+(b+c). This post looks at what happens when integer addition, which is exact, is used.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)

It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

items.title: SpaceX's Starfall just went from secret to storefront (16 minute read)
items.summary: SpaceX has launched a commercial page for Starfall, a disk-shaped reentry capsule that can carry up to 1,000 kg of payload. The capsule can supply 1 kW of power and connect to the internet through Starlink, allowing researchers to pull data from experiments while in orbit instead of waiting for splashdown. It can be used for manufacturing, research, or testing and is aimed at biomedical customers, pharmaceutical companies, and materials science research. Starfall's timeline will depend on Starship - SpaceX is preparing for Flight 15, where it aims to catch both stages with the launch tower.

items.title: Apple Cuts Internal AI Usage Budgets in Move to Reduce Spending (5 minute read)
items.summary: Apple quietly lowered the daily spending cap on AI models for its employees last month. Some engineers had their budgets cut from $300 to $200, and the company is planning further cuts for some engineering teams that may potentially reduce their daily allowances to as little as $100. items.title: The Stacks Project, formalized in Lean (13 minute read)

The release is the largest integrated, reusable library of formalized mathematics ever built. It makes the full mathematical development of the Stacks Project available as a single, machine-checked library that researchers and AI agents can import from directly into new formal proofs.
